description: We are a multidisciplinary team based in Cochabamba, Bolivia, focused on software engineering, web development, and data-driven problem solving. We're tackling the NASA Space Apps Challenge using agile prototyping and modern web tech. We're looking for teammates with skills in Data Analysis or research to join us!
summary:
The City of Cochabamba, Bolivia, encompasses 15 municipal districts but operates only 2 physical environmental monitoring stations, leaving 87% of its territory unmonitored. During winter, a 2,750 m mountain boundary traps particulate matter (PM2.5 > 88 µg/m³) and heat in the valley floor.

Addressing NASA's "Be An Earth System Trend Detective!" challenge, Team Stevens developed a geospatial AI platform that fuses 25 years of NASA orbital data (POWER, MODIS, VIIRS, and FIRMS) with the city's 2 physical stations and 4 official municipal WMS layers (EPSG:3857). 

Our XGBoost 3.2.0 model deploys 13 Virtual Sensors (R² = 0.9457, MAE = 0.44 °C), proving a statistically significant +17.4 °C thermal disparity (Mann-Kendall, p = 0.0000) between the forested mountain and the arid south. The platform features an interactive biometeorological simulator (PET) that empowers city planners to prioritize native tree reforestation and cool pavements.
details:
WHAT IT DOES & HOW IT WORKS:

NASA Trend Detective is an interactive web platform and AI engine that bridges global NASA earth observations with municipal cadastral GIS to eliminate urban climate blind spots. The application directly consumes 4 official municipal WMS layers from the City of Cochabamba (GAMC) in native EPSG:3857 (District Boundaries, Cota 2750 Protection Border, Population by Blocks, and Green Areas). When a user clicks on any city block, the system executes parallel GetFeatureInfo requests under 300 ms to retrieve demographic density, vegetation coverage, and altitudinal protection status.

BENEFITS & INTENDED IMPACT:

Cochabamba is a topographically closed mountain basin where thermal inversion traps toxic smoke and heat. By training an Extreme Gradient Boosting Regressor (XGBoost 3.2.0) on 125,865 hourly ground-truth records from the 2 active municipal stations and 2,497 days of NASA POWER reanalysis, the system generates 13 Virtual AI Stations covering the unmonitored districts at zero hardware cost—saving the city over $1.5M USD. The platform features an Urban Mitigation Simulator that computes Physiological Equivalent Temperature (PET) energy balances, demonstrating that a 30% increase in native trees (Molle and Jacarandá) drops surface LST by 3.2 °C and transitions human heat stress from "Extreme" (>41 °C PET) to "Comfort" (26 °C PET).

TOOLS, LANGUAGES & SOFTWARE USED:

• Frontend & GIS: React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet, GeoJSON, Lucide Icons, and CartoDB/OpenStreetMap/Esri tiles without commercial watermarks.

• Data Science & Machine Learning: Python 3.11, XGBoost 3.2.0, Scikit-learn (TimeSeriesSplit 5-fold cross-validation), Scipy (Mann-Kendall test, Sen's slope, OLS linear regression), Statsmodels (STL Loess decomposition), Pandas, and NumPy.

• Cloud & Hosting: Deployed on Vercel with Offline-First client caching for disaster response centers.

CREATIVITY & SCIENTIFIC RIGOR:

We conducted an Ablation Study proving that incorporating wildfire aerosol optical depth (AOD) from the Tunari mountain reduces predictive error by 39% (RMSE drops from 0.68 °C to 0.55 °C, R² increases from 0.914 to 0.946). This scientifically captures the physical radiative trap of thermal inversion. Following NASA SeaWiFS paper NTRS 20090042747, we decomposed 25-year time series to isolate seasonal cycles from genuine decadal warming (+0.78 °C/decade in southern districts with p = 0.0000 < 0.05). Furthermore, our interactive 3D Planetary Explorer allows any city worldwide to replicate this virtual sensing methodology.
